question.knowledge_point: Finding the Center of a Vertical Hyperbola
question.problem: What is the center of the hyperbola $\frac{(y-7)^{2}}{9}-(x+4)^{2}=1?$
question.worked_solution:
The equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

Note that the given equation can be rewritten as follows:

$$
\frac{(y-7)^{2}}{9}-\frac{(x-(-4))^{2}}{1}=1
$$

In this case, we have $h=-4$ and $k=7.$

Therefore, the center of the hyperbola is $(-4,7).$

question.knowledge_point: Integrating Quotients Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution
question.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

So, let $u=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $-1$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)$ | $1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)}^{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)}^{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1))-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1))\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Parametrizing a Horizontal Parabola Whose Vertex Is at the Origin
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14030835/assets/85894c676349da1794c2b4e3ab3add867fbe9e91037bee060e3592039c3850cf.png)

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?
question.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is horizontal, has its vertex at $(0,0),$ and passes through the point $(-4,4).$

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=p{t}^{2},\,y=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(-4,4),$ we can substitute $x=-4$ and $y=4$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}-4=p{t}^{2} \\ 4=2pt.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the second equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2pt \\ 2 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =p{(\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ -4 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ -4 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=(-1){t}^{2},\,y=2(-1)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=-{t}^{2},\,y=-2t.
$$

question.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation ${y}^{2}=16x?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola ${y}^{2}=4px$ that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=p{t}^{2},\,y=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case ${y}^{2}=4px$ and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4px & =16x \\ 4p & =16 \\ p & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=(4){t}^{2},\,y=2(4)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=4{t}^{2},\,y=8t.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Area Bounded Between the X-Axis and a Curve
question.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=4{x}^{3}+4$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=1.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}+4 & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =-1 \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-1$ is our only real solution. Since $-1\in [-2,1]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=-1.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14030836/assets/b0f2899bf6a946f6d7bf8bc60c41827bd05aef500f0fc0f30a5916c26b1007bb.png)

Notice that the region for $x\in [-2,-1]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{-1}(4{x}^{3}+4)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{-2}^{-1}(4{x}^{3}+4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4{\int }_{-2}^{-1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x-4{\int }_{-2}^{-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{x}^{4}{|}_{-2}^{-1}-4x{|}_{-2}^{-1} \\  & =-[(-1)^{4}-(-2)^{4}]-4[-1+2] \\  & =-(-15)-4 \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [-1,1]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(4{x}^{3}+4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+4{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{4}{|}_{-1}^{1}+4x{|}_{-1}^{-1} \\  & =[{1}^{4}-(-1)^{4}]+4[1-(-1)] \\  & =0+8 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=11+8=19.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Area Bounded Between the X-Axis and a Curve
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14030836/assets/47e15993f3957fb3c1d7619fcf62544b2d5b358715538e17b9232dec5a0172c7.png)

Find the total area of the region between the curve $y={x}^{4}-1$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=2$, as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{4}-1 & =0 \\ {x}^{4} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution between $x=0$ and $x=2$ is $x=1.$

Since $1\in [0,2]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=2.$

Notice that the region for $x\in [0,1]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}-x)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-[\frac{1}{5}-1]-0 \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [1,2]$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}-x)|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =([\frac{32}{5}-2]-[\frac{1}{5}-1]) \\  & =\frac{26}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{4}{5}+\frac{26}{5}=\frac{30}{5}=6.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Definite Integral of Function Using Substitution
question.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =8x+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =8 \\ \text{d}u & =8\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{8}\text{d}u & =\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=8x+1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & \frac{1}{4} \\ u & 1 & 3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1/4}\sqrt{8x+1}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{3}\sqrt{u}\,\cdot \frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}\sqrt{u}\,\cdot \frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{3}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot \frac{2}{3}({3}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}({({3}^{3})}^{1/2}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(3\sqrt{3}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding Local Minima and Local Maxima of Polynomials
question.problem: For which value of $x$ does the function $f(x)=12x+9{x}^{2}-4{x}^{3}$ have a local maximum?
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the stationary points. Differentiating $f(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =12+18x-12{x}^{2} \\  & =-6(2{x}^{2}-3x-2) \\  & =-6(x-2)(2x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ gives

$$
-6(x-2)(2x+1)=0\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2},2.
$$

So we have two stationary points, $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $x=2.$ Next, to determine whether these points are local maxima or minima, we use the first derivative test.

Let's choose the test points $x=-1,0,3$ and evaluate the first derivative at these points.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-1) & =-6(-1-2)(2(-1)+1)=-18<0 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =-6(0-2)(2(0)+1)=12>0 \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =-6(3-2)(2(3)+1)=-42<0\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize the information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-\frac{1}{2})$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $(-\frac{1}{2},2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $-1$ |  | $0$ |  | $3$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ | min | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

Finally, let's use the table above to classify the critical points.

- At $x=-\frac{1}{2},$ the first derivative changes sign from negative to positive. Therefore, $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ is a local minimum.

- At $x=2,$ the first derivative changes sign from positive to negative. Therefore, $x=2$ is a local maximum.

We conclude that $f(x)$ has one local maximum at $x=2.$

choices.value: $f(x)$ does not have any local maxima

question.problem: For which value of $x$ does the function $f(x)=\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡x}{x}$ defined for $x\in (0,\infty )$ have a local maximum?
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
f(x)=\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡x}{x}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡(10)}.
$$

Now, we find the stationary points. Differentiating $f(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{(\frac{1}{x}\cdot x\operatorname{ln}⁡(10)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(10)\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}{ln}^{2}⁡(10)} \\  & =\frac{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(10)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ on $(0,\infty )$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(10)} & =0 \\ 1-\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡x & =1 \\ x & =e.\end{aligned}
$$

So $x=e$ is a stationary point. Next, to determine whether this point is a local maximum or minimum, we use the first derivative test.

Let's choose the test points $x=1,{e}^{2}$ and evaluate the first derivative at these points.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)}{(1)^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(10)}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(10)}>0 \\ {f}^{′}({e}^{2}) & =\frac{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})}{(e)^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(10)}=-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(10)}<0\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize the information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,e)$ | $e$ | $(e,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ |  | ${e}^{2}$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $f$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

Finally, let's use the table above to classify the critical point.

- At $x=e,$ the first derivative changes sign from positive to negative. Therefore, $x=e$ is a local maximum.

We conclude that $f(x)$ has a local maximum at $x=e.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14031229/assets/59704c6b8e643337113ab99b22eaeaac8d59ac3c15042409e8a0a8eac6ee54fd.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\frac{t}{2},\,y={e}^{t}$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ (shown above)?
question.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have
We have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2})=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{({e}^{2t})+(\frac{1}{4})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}+1}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Not a Polynomial
question.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=-\frac{4}{(2+t)^{2}}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s}$, find the velocity (in $\text{m}/\text{s}$) of the particle at time $t.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-\frac{4}{(2+t)^{2}})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{2+t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\frac{4}{2+0}+C \\ 2 & =2+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{4}{2+t}.$

question.problem: Find the number $c>0$ such that the average value of $f(x)=9+8x-3{x}^{2}$ on the interval $[0,c]$ is equal to $-3.$
question.worked_solution:
To solve for $c,$ we apply the average value formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}\,{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ -3 & =\frac{1}{c-0}\,{\int }_{0}^{c}(9+8x-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ -3 & =\frac{1}{c}(9x+4{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}){|}_{0}^{c} \\ -3 & =\frac{1}{c}[(9c+4{c}^{2}-{c}^{3})-(0)] \\ -3 & =9+4c-{c}^{2} \\ {c}^{2}-4c-12 & =0 \\ (c+2)(c-6) & =0 \\ c & =-2,\,6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $c>0,$ we conclude that $c=6$ only.

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Moment in Time When a Particle is Stationary
question.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}-6t+10),\,t\ge 0.
$$

Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary.
question.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}-6t+10)) \\  & =\frac{2t-6}{{t}^{2}-6t+10} \\  & =\frac{2(t-3)}{{t}^{2}-6t+10}\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m/s}.$ So, we set $v=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2(t-3)}{{t}^{2}-6t+10} & =0 \\ 2(t-3) & =0 \\ t & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t=3\,\text{s}.$
